top_choice_rationale: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock is a distinct, original idea (state-independent trapping of many neutral atoms on a narrow transition) that is mature, reproduced in several independent laboratories at the 10^-18 level, and already used in relativistic geodesy and tests of varying constants. Katori and Ye is the cleanest two-name allocation, and a citation worded around the lattice and many-atom interrogation, not accuracy in general, separates it from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes. The unresolved Takamoto/Hong/Ludlow/Lemke first-demonstration credit is a real caveat but does not outweigh the achievement, so a prize is preferable to no award.
recusal_note: No direct connection to Katori or Ye apparent from profile; as a superconducting-circuit and quantum-computing theorist and WACQT director at Chalmers, I have no documented tie to optical lattice clocks.
